F.M.A. No. 81 of 2005
F.M.A.T. No. 70 of 2005
lawyer:
Mr. Mrinal Kanti Biswas, Advocate ----- For the appellant. 
Mr. Md. Khalilur Rahman with Mr. T.M. Shakil Hasan, Advocates ----- For the respondents.
parties:
Pubali Bank Ltd.
Vs.
Contech Ltd. and others
full_judgment:
Syed Amirul Islam, J: This Miscellaneous Appeal is taken up for hearing along with an application for vacating the stay filed by the plaintiff-respondents (hereinafter called 'the respondents'). This miscellaneous appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 30.11.2004 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Dhaka, in Title Suit No. 227 of 2004 passing an order to maintain status quo in respect of the mortgaged property of the defendant-respondents till the disposal of the suit. 

 2. The relevant facts in short are that the defendant-appellant (hereinafter called 'the appellant') filed Arthor Rin Adalat Case No. 33 of 2002 against the respondents for realising an amount of Tk. 39 lac and odd. The respondents contested the suit by filing written statement. The aforesaid suit was for realisation of unpaid loan amount that was taken by the respondents from the appellant bank. In that case the respondents in their written statement though admitted the loan liability but came up with a specific plea that in view of the facts and circumstances of the case and in view of the undertaking given by the Siemens Bangladesh Limited (hereinafter called 'the Siemens') confirming that all payment arising out of work order issued by the Social Marketing Company Ltd (hereinafter called 'the SMC') vide their letter dated 14.12.1998, would be made directly by the Siemens to the bank, the appellant. The defence taken by the respondent in Artho Rin Case is more or less is the case as made out by the respondent in Title Suit No. 227 of 2004. The crux of the case of the respondents was that they entered into a bilateral agreement with Siemens for the aforesaid work order and since Siemens was the lead firm no tripartite agreement could be entered into in respect of the said work order. The purpose of the loan was known to the bank and they initially insisted upon the respondents to enter into a tripartite agreement with the bank and Siemens but since the work order was issued in the name of the lead firm it was not possible to comply with the request of the bank. Therefore, both before and after sanctioning of the loan the appellant insisted upon the respondents for obtaining a confirmation from the lead firm, namely the defendant-respondent No. 6 of the present appeal to give an undertaking to the bank that whatever amount is withdrawn as bill would be enroute through Siemens and would be directly deposited with the account of the respondents to liquidate their liabilities. The further case is that before and after giving of the loan Seimens confirmed in writing to the bank that they would directly remit the amount to the account of the respondents. The further case of the respondents is that the Siemens, the defendant respondent of the present appeal made part payment on two occasions and thereafter when the project was completed and full payment was realised by the Siemens they in collusion with the bank did not make any further payment and withhold that money even after receipt of final payment from the SMC. It is contended in the plaint that the respondents did not make any query with the bank about their liquidation or repayment of the liability of the loan amount as it was agreed between the parties that the money would be deposited with the account of the respondents. Therefore, the present respondents in the Arthorin case No. 33 of 2002 took the plea that the balance unpaid amount of the loan is to be paid by the Siemens who had given unconditional undertaking to the bank to repay the loan amount out of the share of the respondents arising out of the aforesaid work order. This plea of the respondents in the Arthorin Case failed as the learned Arthorin Adalat took the view that since the loan was taken by the respondents they are legally bound to repay the same and the application filed by the respondents for impleading Siemens as defendant in the Artho Rin Adalat case was rejected. The Arthorin Adalat allows the financial institution to institute suit for realisation of loan amount from the defaulters including the mortgagor and the guarantor of the loan. Since Siemens did not fall within the definition of either mortgagor or guarantor the plea of 'defect of parties' was rejected by the Arthorin Adalat. Therefore, in decreeing Arthorin Adalat Case No. 33 of 2002 the view taken by the Arthorin Adalat is that he is only to decide as to whether the defendants of the suit who are the plaintiffs in the present suit had taken the loan and if the answer is in the affirmative then the suit would not be found to be defect of parties and admittedly in the instant case the loan was taken by the respondents who were the defendants in Arthorin Adalat Case and since the liability of the loan was not denied the case was decreed by the Arthorin Adalat and it further appears that after obtaining the said decree the bank has instituted Execution Case No. 338 of 2004 in the said Arthorin Adalat and in the meantime the defendants of the Arthorin Adalat case instead of preferring any appeal before the High Court Division filed the present Title Suit namely- Title Suit No. 227 of 2004 in the Court of 5th Joint District Judge, Dhaka, on the pleadings that they do not deny the liability of the loan but in view of the undisputed fact that Siemens gave an undertaking to repay the loan amount on behalf of the plaintiffs it was the duty of the defendant bank to realise the said amount directly from the Siemens instead of the plaintiffs of the present suit but the defendant bank being in collusion with the Siemens did not make any earnest effort to realise the loan amount from the Siemens rather they played a foul game and after the expiry of the loan period, i.e., after 31.12.2000 it is only in August, 2001 the defendant bank was in touch with the plaintiff that the Siemens did not pay the amount and therefore they asked the present defendant to repay the loan amount and the stand taken by the plaintiffs in the instant suit as well as in the Arthorin Adalat Case is that since at the instance of the bank an undertaking was given by Siemens to repay the loan amount it was the duty of the bank to realise the same from the Siemens and in the event of default to institute suit for realisation of the same from Siemens as principal defendant and the respondent as proforma defendant but the bank instead of doing so in collusion with the Siemens have instituted the Arthorin Adalat Case against the present respondents to give some benefits to the Siemens and also to harass the present respondents for no fault of them. The present suit has been instituted by the plaintiff-respondents claiming the following relieves, namely — that the letter dated 29.8.2001 issued by the defendant No.1, i.e. Siemens to defendant Nos. 2-3 the plaintiffs' Bank to submit bill to it through the plaintiff being contrary with the undertaking given by Siemens dated 15.9.1999 is collusive, mala fide, fraudulent, illegal and not binding upon the plaintiffs. The plaintiff-respondents also made a further prayer by way of declaration that the defendant No. 1 Siemens is bound to pay the decreetal amount of Tk. 39,34,740/-and other liabilities of decree passed in Arthorin Adalat Case No. 33 of 2002 and the plaintiff respondents also made claim for compensation to the tune of Tk. 5,50,00,000/- against all the defendants in that suit. We have already indicated that in the meantime the defendant bank have instituted Execution Case to realise the decreetal amount against the present plaintiff and in that view of. the matter after institution of the suit the plaintiff respondents filed an application for injunction under order 39 rules 1 and 2 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure (hereinafter called 'the Code'). That application was opposed by the bank by filing' a written objection and after hearing both the parties the learned Trial Court passed an order against the defendant bank to maintain status quo in respect of the properties mortgaged by the plaintiffs as security to the loan given by the bank earlier. 

 3. After the admission of the instant miscellaneous appeal the defendant-appellant filed an application for stay of the impugned order and this Court vide order dated 29.3.2005 stayed the impugned order along with the further proceedings of the instant suit initially for two months whereupon the plaintiff-respondents have come up with an application for vacating the order of stay. The present defendant-appellants also filed a supplementary affidavit-in-opposition opposing the prayer for vacating the order of stay. 

 6. Mr. Mrinal Kanti Biswas, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant submits that the instant suit is misconceived and not tenable in law inasmuch as the averments which have been made in the plaint of the present suit was exactly the contention that has been raised by the present plaintiffs as defendants in Arthorin Adalat Case No. 33 of 2002 and that contention was negetived by the Arthorin Adalat holding that Siemens is not a necessary party. The learned Advocate further submits that the relieves sought for clearly indicate that these are in fact claim in terms of money and therefore one of the vital elements to get an order of injunction is that the alleged injury must be an irreparable injury which is not calculable in terms of money and all of the relieves that have been claimed by the respondents indicate that these are nothing but monetary relieves. Therefore, they have miserably failed to make out the case of irreparable loss which disentitle them to get an order of injunction in their favour. The learned advocate further submits that the respondents do not deny the liability of the loan and they also do not dispute the decreetal amount. All that they do is that the money is to be paid to the bank not by the loanee, i.e., the respondents but by Siemens which is not a loanee from the bank. Therefore the defendant bank even if tried to realise the money from the Seimens their claim would have been denied by the Siemens inasmuch as there is no privity between the bank and Siemens in respect of the instant loan. In spite of that the bank tried their level best to realise their money from the Siemens pursuant to the undertaking given by them and it is only when their efforts failed they have brought it to the notice of the appellant about the liability vide their letter dated 29.8.2001 and in spite of that letter the respondents did not take any steps whatsoever to liquidate their liability. Therefore, this conduct of the respondents also disentitles them to make a prayer for an order of injunction inasmuch as an injunction is nothing but an equitable relief and it is well settled that he who seeks equity must do equity and in the instant case the respondents are guilty of negligence and laches to repay loan liability. Therefore, on this count also the prayer for injunction ought to have been refused by the Trial Court. The learned Advocate further submits that the instant suit has been filed by the plaintiff-respondents with the sole motive of frustrating the fruits of the decree that have been obtained by the Bank after much delay and long after the expiry of the date of repayment of the loan and at huge expenses and by instituting the suit the respondents are in fact trying to get a relief indirectly which they are not entitle to get directly. Therefore, in that view of the matter also not only that they have failed to make out a prima facie case but also the plaint of the suit is liable to be rejected under order 7 rule 11 of the code. The learned Advocate further submits that the impugned order suffers from patent illegality and infirmity inasmuch as by passing an order of status quo which is in fact an order of injunction the appellant have been handicapped in proceeding with the execution case and this impugned order frustrated the decree of the Arthorin Adalat and these vital aspects were overlooked by the Trial Court in granting the order of status quo. The learned Advocate further submits that the impugned order also offends the provision of section 37 of the Arthorin Adalat Ain inasmuch as a time frame has been given by the Parliament for executing a decree of Arthorin Adalat i.e., the execution proceeding must be initiated within 90 days of the decree and that dead time has been fixed for speedy satisfaction of the decreetal amount as Banks deal with public money and the impugned order has put the decree in uncertainty and this aspect has been overlooked by the Trial Court in passing the impugned order. The learned Advocate 

 7. Mr. Khalilur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondents, on the other hand, submits that in the instant suit the respondents do not deny the loan liability and their only case is that the purpose of the loan was known to the defendant bank and it was known to them before sanctioning the loan that the loan is taken for carrying out the work order that would be issued by the defendant No. 4 for installation of electric substation and a generator at defendant No.4's head office at Banani. It is also within the knowledge of the appellant bank that the Seimens was the lead firm and since they entered into a contract with SMC there was no possibility of entering into a tripartite agreement' in respect of the loan amount amongst bank, the respondents and Siemens and that is why in addition of taking colateral security by way of mortgage of the personal property of the Chairman and Director of Contech Ltd. they also insisted upon the respondents to take an undertaking from Siemens, i.e. the respondent No. 6 to make the payment directly to the bank on account of the said work order in the account of Contech Ltd. The learned advocate referring to the letters written by the Siemens on 18.5.1998 to the Divisional Manager and Commercial Manager of the Bank they have stated that they would issue a certificate to whom it may concern mentioning that they will pay all portions of the bill of Contech Ltd. through Pubali Bank, Satmasjid Road, Dhaka, in the account of Contech Ltd. and also by a letter dated 18.5.98 informed the Managing Director of Contech Ltd. that they confirmed that all payments in connection with supply of the generator in the joint venture would be made directly to the Pubali Bank, Satmasjid road, Dhaka, as requested by Contech Ltd. copy of which was also forwarded to the Manager of the aforesaid branch of Pubali Bank whereupon the defendant bank vide their letter dated 8.6.99 requested the Siemens to issue cheques payable to M/S. Contech Ltd. In the sanction letter dated 9.6.99 in paragraph No. 4(iii) it was laid down that an undertaking from Siemens has to be obtained by the respondents to effect payment through cheques/bills direct to Pubali Bank, Satmasjid Road Branch, Dhaka, against value of work order for Tk. 19 lac awarded by SMC and in pursuance of that condition the Siemens vide their letter dated 15.6.99 confirmed that all payments in connection with supply of generator arising out of the work order issued by the SMC under joint venture agreement would be made directly to Pubali Bank Ltd, Satmasjid Road, Dhaka, in the account of Contech Ltd. and relying on these admitted documents Mr. Khalilur Rahman emphatically submits that it does not lie in the mouth of the defendant-appellant bank that Siemens has no privy in the contract. Mr. Rahman submits that the purpose of taking loan was well within the knowledge of the bank and in order to secure the repayment of loan amount the Bank not only took mortgage of the personal property of the Director of Contech Ltd but also insisted upon the Contech to take an undertaking from the Siemens to make the payment directly of their portion of the work order to the bank and the Siemens vide their letter dated 15.6.99 in clear terms given the undertaking that all payments would be made directly to the bank as desired by the bank. Mr. Khalilur Rahman then submits that in the instant case the admitted position is that that agreement has been acted upon by Siemens and in furtherance of their undertaking two part payments were made by Siemens to the bank, one on 29.6.99 for Tk. 46,000/- and odd and the other on 9.12.99 for a further amount of Tk. 18 lac and odd and at that time balance stood at Tk. 20,84,172/-. Therefore, it was the legal obligation of the defendant bank to realise the balance amount directly from Siemens and ought not have fallen back on the respondents inasmuch as the undertaking was accepted by the bank as one of the conditions of sanctioning the loan. Therefore, in the circumstances of the case there was, in fact, an oral tripartite agreement amongst the bank, the respondents and the Siemens and law does not require that all agreements must be in writing. It is well settled that an agreement can be wholly oral, partly oral and partly written and wholly in writing and in the instant case the materials on record clearly indicate that there is a tripartite agreement based on oral as well as written documents. Therefore, in instituting the Arthorin Case No. 33 of 2002 it was the legal obligation of the bank to implead Siemens as the principal defendant but their omission to add them as a party even after the objection raised by the present appellant in their written statement in that suit clearly smacks of mala fide and collusion between Siemens and bank. The learned Advocate further submits that neither in the Arthorin case nor in the present suit the appellant could make out a case that they are not bound to pursue the Siemens in realising the balance amount pursuant to the undertaking given by Siemens at the instance of the bank both before and after sanctioning of the loan. The learned Advocate further submits that the purpose of institution of the present suit is not' to frustrate the fruits of the decree obtained by the bank in Arthorin Case rather the purpose of the instant suit is to compel the Siemens, who is illegally withholding the money of the plaintiffs, to make payment of that amount to the bank as per share of the plaintiffs to the bank and the decree has never been disputed by the plaintiffs at any stage. They had neither denied their liability in the Arthorin Case nor they have denied the liability in the instant case rather their case is that it is the Siemens who are liable to pay the money which have been illegally held by the Siemens after taking the payment from SMC. Mr. Rahman to bring home his contention of collusion and/or mala fide refers to certain communications made by the bank with Siemens and referring to those letters he submits that these were secret communications made by the bank with the Siemens keeping the respondents in dark and previously on two occasions before completion of the work order as and when cheques were withdrawn by the lead firm Siemens they had made payments directly to the bank. Therefore, in all goodness and bona fide the plaintiffs saw that since the Siemens has given an undertaking to make the payment and bank also has accepted the undertaking to realise the amount they would, in due, course realise the same from Siemens on final payment and that is why they did not feel it necessary at any stage of proceeding about the loan liability as their liability was taken by Siemens on their shoulder and if now they default in making the payment in all fairness in terms of the tripartite agreement they ought to have pursue the Siemens for making the payment and not the present respondents. The learned Advocate further submits that neither in the Arthorin Case nor from the averments made in the plaint of the instant suit it can be said that the respondents have ever defaulted in carrying out their obligation under the contract and that by obtaining of unequivocal undertaking and confirmation from Siemens in fact and in the eye of law the respondents have shifted their liability to the shoulder of Siemens who voluntarily accepted the same. Therefore, in the event of failure on the part of Siemens it does not lie in the mouth of the bank to pay the decreetal amount setting free the real culprit, i.e. the Siemens. The learned advocate further submits that one of the requests of not making any enquiry with the bank as to the liability of the loan so that the undertaking given by Siemens is still in force and therefore the respondents were under the impression that if for any reason Siemens defaults the bank would, in the ordinary course of business, make payment but it appears that the bank keeping the respondents in the dark conspired with the Siemens and getting some financial benefit shifted the burden on to the shoulder of the innocent respondents. Mr. Khalilur Rahman then submits that though apparently it appears that the plea taken by the respondents in the instant suit is one and same as has been taken in the written statement of the Arthorin Adalat case but on a second reading it appears that in the instant suit the petitioner has claimed a relief against the real defaulter and to compel him to carry out his legal obligation as he undertook by giving an undertaking to the bank and moreover the issues in the instant case are altogether different from the issues of the Arthrin Adalat Case inasmuch as here the respondents want to enforce the legal obligation that has been created in his favour by the appellant the Siemens Bangladesh Ltd. and the same plea before the Arthorin Adalat Case failed but for a technicality of law and the Arthorin Adalat did not or could not go to decide that issue for want of jurisdiction. Therefore, although the factual aspect made Up to be similar in both the cases but it was assumed different dimension in the instant suit. Therefore, by no stretch of imagination it could be said that the instant suit is either barred by the principles of estoppel and/or by doctrine of estoppel. The learned advocate further submits that it is now well settled that in order to get a favourable order of injunction under order 39 rules 1 and 2 the petitioner requires to establish a prima facie case and prima facie case in the context of order 39 appears to be an issue raising a serious question of law and in the instant suit which is peculiar in nature has arose a very complicated and unique issue which has now been raised in this jurisdiction. The learned Advocate further submits that if the averments made by the respondents in the plaint and the 

 contention made by the defendant-appellants are considered in the light of the admitted documents that have been filed before this Court it would be clear that the respondents have been able to establish a strong prima facie case and in the facts and circumstances of the case at this stage it cannot be said that any amount of certainty that the plaintiff have no chance to succeed in the suit. The learned Advocate further submits that it is true on a perusal of the relieves claimed in the plaint that it mainly relates to monitory compensation and claim but if the way goes deep into the issues it shows us that these claims in fact is clearly related with the immovable properties that have been mortgaged by the respondents at the time of taking the loan from the bank. Therefore, although in the suit there is a claim in terms of money but it is deeply linked with the immovable property of the respondents. Therefore, Mr. Khalilur Rahman contends that in such a situation if the mortgaged property including the dwelling house are sold in execution of the Arthorin decree the respondents will suffer irreparable loss even if at the end of the day the suit successfully terminates in their favour and in that situation they will have some amount of money but will never be able to get back the property which will be sold in execution of the Arthorin Adalat decree. Therefore, it will cause irreparable loss and injury. 

 8. Mr. Mrinal Kanti Biswas in the course of argument tried to assail the impugned order on the ground that the Trial Court by granting an order of maintaining status quo has given a relief to the plaintiff-appellants which is altogether different from the relief claimed by the plaintiff-appellants in their suit. To refute the same he submits that it is now well settled that the ultimate say in such a situation rests with the court and in an appropriate case in the interest of justice and fair play this Court is empowered always to pass an order which it deems fit and proper in the given facts and circumstances and in the instant case the facts and circumstances are so peculiar that without restraining the defendant-appellants no proper justice would be done to the plaintiffs in the instant case. The learned advocate further submits that in instituting the present suit the respondents are wide conscious about the provisions of law as contained in section 56(k) of the Specific Relief Act in that no Court can be injuncted upon to proceed with any proceeding but it is now well settled that although a court cannot be injuncted upon but nevertheless a party can be restrained by granting injunction not to proceed with the proceedings in any court and thus in the instant case the respondents are not praying for restraining the Arthorin Adalat not to proceed with the execution case rather the instant suit has been filed to realise the decreetal amount from the real debtor, namely — the Siemens Bangladesh Limited. 

 9. This is a case which not only raises a noble and new question of law but the facts and circumstances of the case are also peculiar in nature. We have heard the learned advocates at length and we have also given our thought as much as we can in this case. It appear that in this case we are acquainted with a very special circumstances wherein the respondents do not deny the liability that was created by taking loan from the bank against the work order in question. Their sole grievance against the bank and the respondents is that at the time of taking loan and even after sanctioning of the said loan it was insisted upon by the bank that the Siemens must give undertaking to pay all the cheques for the share of the money of the plaintiffs directly to their account maintained with the bank and it further appears that on two occasions Siemens did carry out their obligation of depositing the cheques directly to the bank. Thereafter in spite of the fact that they have received the final payment from SMC they are not depositing the balance amount of the plaintiffs in their account nor they are in communication with the plaintiffs for non-depositing the said amount. So, the only grievance of the plaintiff is that they have no doubt borrowed the money from the bank but pursuant to the tripartite agreement it is now the Siemens which is liable to pay the amount to the bank and they admittedly defaulted in making the payment. Therefore, it was a duty of the bank to pursue the real defaulter but for reasons best known to them they are pursuing the present respondents leaving aside the real borrower. 

 11. In the course of argument Mr. Khalilur Rahman has never disputed the principles of law laid down in the decisions referred to and relied on by Mr. Biswas but he contended that those decisions, in fact, supports the case of the plaintiffs inasmuch as in the facts and circumstances of the case the plaintiffs have been able to prove that they have a strong prima facie arguable case and that if no injunction is granted against the appellant and they are allowed to proceed with the execution case before the Arthorin Adalat that would cause irreparable loss to the plaintiffs and also the balance of convenience and inconvenience is in favour of the plaintiffs. It is now well settled that order 39 rules 1 and 2 are not exhaustive and there are innumerable examples where strictly speaking a case may not come within the ambit of order 39 rules 1 and 2 and this aspect of the case was in the back of the mind of the legislature when they enacted the Code of Civil Procedure in 1908 and that is why the Parliament was prompted to incorporate section 94(c) in the Code to cover a situation in a given set of facts to grant injunction in the interest of justice if it is not covered by order 39 rules 1 and 2. This section 94 has been interpreted by Indian Supreme Court in the case reported in AIR 1962 (SC) 527 and in interpreting the section the Indian Supreme Court observed that "if it is so prescribed" in section 94 of the Code means rules framed under order 39. The Indian Supreme Court is of opinion that in a given circumstance of the case strictly speaking if it does not come within the ambit of order 39 rules 1 and 2 then the Court for the ends of justice can grant injunction invoking its jurisdiction under section 94 (c) of the Code and the Indian Supreme Court went one step further that is even if in a case it is found that it does not come either under order 39 rules 1 and 2 or section 94(c) in that case the Court is not helpless but is empowered to exercise its inherent power and it is now well settled that the provisions of section 151 .i.e., ex debito justitiae means Court can do what it requires to do in the interest of justice and it is now well settled in all the jurisdictions that section 151 did not, in fact, confer any inherent power on the Court rather it is inherent in the court itself and this aspect of the case has been well considered by our Appellate Division in the case reported in 35 DLR (AD) 42 wherein it has been observed by our Appellate Division that if the facts and circumstances of a case do not come within the ambit of order 39 rule 1 in that case always the court can exercise its inherent power, not only in making prohibitory injunction but can also pass an order of mandatory injunction in temporary form under order 39 and that view expressed by the Appellate Division has been reiterated by our Appellate Division in the latest decision reported in 47 DLR (AD) 7. Therefore, it is now beyond any doubt that this Court sitting in its civil jurisdiction can pass an order which it thinks just and proper in the given facts and circumstances of the case. 

 12. Keeping these principle in the back of our mind let us now examine the legal issues as have been raised by the learned advocates of both the parties. According to Mr. Biswas the plaintiffs have miserably failed to make out a prima facie case and filed the suit with the ill motive of delaying the execution of the decree obtained by the bank in the Arthorin Adalat case. Let us see if there is any substance in this contention. We have gone through the judgment of Arthorin Adalat. On a perusal of the judgment it becomes crystal clear that in that suit in the written statement the present plaintiff had admitted the liability of the loan. Their sole contention in that case was that due to the arrangement made amongst the bank and the Siemens it was the liability of the Siemens to pay the balance amount. Therefore they contended in that Arthorin case that the case suffers from defect of parties for non-impleading Siemens as a defendant. However, that contention was rejected by the Arthorin Adalat by taking a view that Arthorin Adalat will see if the case is filed by the financial institution against loanee, mortgagee or guarantor of a loan and according to the Arthorin Adalat the Siemens did not come within the description of guarantor, loanee or mortgagee. Therefore, the Arthorin Adalat observed that the case does not suffer from any defect of parties. Here we are not sitting in the appellate jurisdiction and as such need not advert to the judgment of the Arthorin Adalat. Therefore, we do not want to express any opinion as to the view taken by the Arthorin Adalat in that judgment although in our view there is scope of taking a different view. Thus after the passing of the Arthorin Adalat Judgment the respondents were confronted with a helpless situation for no fault of them according to their version. The plaintiffs have admitted the liability and till today it is the case of the bank that the loan which was due to the plaintiffs has been repaid by the Siemens directly to the bank by depositing the cheques to the plaintiff's account maintained with the bank but at this stage it appears that the Siemens in breach of their undertaking, are illegally withholding a substantial amount of money which fell in the share of the plaintiffs and they instead of depositing the money in the account of the plaintiffs are enjoying the same without carrying out their obligation. Therefore, to get out of this helpless situation when the plaintiffs found it difficult for them to file an appeal against Arthorin decree as they could do so only by depositing 50% of the decreetal amount they had resorted to the instant suit and in the instant suit what is the issue? The issue is that the Siemens under the terms of the undertaking is still liable to pay the amount to the bank and they without making the payment to the bank are withholding the payment and retaining the money of the plaintiffs and using the same in their business in collusion with the dishonest officials of the bank. Therefore, in order to carry out the obligation pursuant to the decree of the Arthorin case they had no other alternative but to institute the instant suit. We have carefully examined the admitted papers which have been filed by the parties and here is a singular instance where none of the documents submitted has been disputed by either of the parties. So on scrutiny of the admitted documents it appears that before giving loan bank wanted an assurance from Siemens that they should give an undertaking on behalf of the Contech Ltd. to make the payment of their share of the money directly to the bank and this negotiation took place prior to the sanction of the loan and there was correspondence between the bank, Contech Ltd. and Siemens and at the instance of the bank the plaintiffs wrote a letter to Siemens to issue a certificate mentioning that they will pay all the portions of the bill of the plaintiffs through the account of Contech Ltd. of Pubali Bank, Satmasjid Road, Dhaka. From Annexure '3', i.e. letter dated 18.5.95 it appears that the Siemens wrote a letter to the Contech Ltd. wherein they have confirmed that all payments in connection with supply of generator under joint venture agreement would be made directly to the bank as requested by Contech Ltd. and a copy of that letter was also endorsed by the Manager of the said bank. It further appears from Annexure '4', i.e., the letter dated 8.6.99 written by the bank to Siemens whereby they have given the instruction how to draw the cheque in the name of the plaintiffs and in reply thereto the Siemens by their letter dated 15,6,99 confirmed the bank that all payments in connection with the supply of generator would be directly paid to them as desired by them. It further appears that at the time of sanctioning loan the bank urged upon the plaintiffs that they must obtain an undertaking from Siemens to effect the payment through cheques to the said bank and it appears that Siemens by their letter dated 15.6.99 have confirmed that they would do so. Therefore, a legal question crops up as to whether in the admitted facts and circumstances there is a tripartite agreement in respect of the instant loan. Whether there is a tripartite agreement or not would be pertinent issue to be decided in the suit itself but at this stage in dealing with the injunction matter suffice it to say that on the basis of the materials on record it cannot be said that there is no prima facie case at all. There is another aspect of the case which is as to whether the confirmation given by the Siemens would bring them within the definition of guarantor within the meaning of Arthorin Adalat Act. However, since the matter is not before us we need not advert to that aspect but to see if there is prima facie case it may be taken into consideration. The admitted position is that to get an order of temporary injunction the petitioner has to show that he has a prima facie case and in 26 DLR 157 it has been laid down by a Division Bench of this Court that whether in a given case there is prima facie case or not or a serious question of law is involved can only be determined by referring to the plaint case. We have/had the opportunity of perusing the plaint and the admitted documents wherefrom we arrive at a finding that in view of the admitted documents it appears to us that the plaintiffs have been able to prove a strong arguable case to go at the trial. This is a unique noble question of law to our 

 knowledge has been raised for the first time in this case which needs close scrutiny of law. Therefore, we are of the view that the plaintiff-respondents have been able to cross the first hurdle of prima facie case. Then it brings us to the second element of injunction, namely — the question of irreparable loss. Mr. Biswas very emphatically submitted drawing our attention to the terms of the relief prayed for by the plaintiffs and submitted that the bird's eye view of the prayer portion of the plaint clearly indicates that it is nothing but a money suit and if it is a money claim that can surely be calculated in terms of money and that sort of injury can never be termed irreparable injury either within the meaning of order 39 rules 1 and 2 or within section 94(c) of the Code. To refute the same Mr. Khalilur Rahman candidly submitted that at no stage of the proceedings either before the Arthorin Adalat or in this Court the plaintiffs have ever denied their liability arising out of the loan , All through both before the Arthorin Adalat and in the instant case their only plea is that in the given set of facts they are not liable to pay the balance. amount of the loan money inasmuch as till to-day the bank could not say that the undertaking given by Siemens have been withdrawn. Therefore, it is the Siemens who are liable to pay the amount but the bank without pursuing Siemens has fallen upon the plaintiff-respondents to realise the amount and to get red of that rigour and to come out of that unjust claim of the bank after the passing of the decree by the Arthorin Adalat they had no other alternative but. to institute the instant suit because they are not at all liable with regard to the repayment of loan. Mr. Khalilur Rahman submitted that superficially it appears that the plaintiffs have sought for relief by way of compensation but that compensation is linked with the immovable property of the respondents which have been mortgaged with the bank and if the bank is allowed to realize the amount by executing the decree through auction sale of his immovable property including the dwelling house of the respondents and at the end of the day a decree is passed in the instant suit in favour of the respondents the injury which would be suffered by the respondents would be an irreparable loss and injury which could not be compensated by any amount of money. With the execution of the decree the respondents will be rendered homeless. They would be thrown out from the dwelling house and even if at the end of the day they get some money that will not be sufficient to repair their injury. Therefore, in the facts and circumstances of the case they had to couch their relieves in such terms as to compel the real debtor to liquidate the liability of the loan amount. We have examined the prayer portion of the plaint and no doubt these are couched in terms of money. What is the prayer No. 1 ? By prayer No.1 the plaintiff-respondents have made letter dated 29.8.2001 written by Siemens to defendant Nos. 2 and 3 as collusive and not binding upon them. Here it would be pertinent to mention to the earlier correspondences made by Siemens with the bank. Before the sanctioning of the loan they had Made it clear to the bank that all cheques would have to be submitted through their bank and will be deposited to the account of Contech Ltd. and pursuant to clause 4(iii) of the loan sanctioning order Siemens has given an unambiguous undertaking that they would pass all the cheques of the plaintiffs to the defendant bank. In these two letters it was never stipulated that the payment of the cheques would be subject to submission of any bill and/or advice made by Contech Ltd. to the Siemens. We have earlier discussed the fact that the admitted position is that the work order was given to Siemens as the Siemens was the lead firm and this loan was taken by the plaintiffs to complete their part of the contract and it was agreed upon that SMC will issue all the cheques in the name of Siemens because Siemens is the lead firm and that is why as per desire of the bank the plaintiffs could not enter into the tripartite agreement as it was not possible in the facts and circumstances of the case and it has been made clear in the earlier correspondences that the share of the plaintiffs would be over taka one crore and bank was satisfied on the undertaking given by Siemens. Mr. Khalilur Rahman in bringing home his allegation of collusion and mala fide has submitted that if we go through these letters it would be clear that the correspondences were made secretly by the bank with the Siemens without giving any copy to the plaintiff-respondents. It appears that in the letter dated 26.2.2000 written by Siemens to the bank they have for the first time asserted that earlier they confirmed to issue all the cheques to the bank in connection with the payment on the basis of advice received from Contech Ltd. It appears to us that this factum of advice has been introduced by Siemens for the first time in their letter dated 26.2.2000 but while giving undertaking on 15.6.99 they have never spelt it out that they will be obliged to pay the cheques on the advice of Contech Ltd. The matter did not end there. It further appears that finally even after receipt of the final bill from SMC they came up with the plea that the balance amount would not be paid to the bank as they have not received any bill from Contech Ltd. and they would make the payment any time if they receive the bill from Contech Ltd. This is also a new fact introduced by Siemens in their letter dated 29.8.2001 well after the expiry of the loan period and long after the receipt of the final payment. We fail to understand why bank did not draw the attention of the Siemens that when they gave the undertaking on 15.6.99 they did not mention that they would issue the cheques as and when they receive the advice from Contech Ltd. and or on receipt of bill from the Contech. Here it appears to us that Mr. Rahman has rightly submitted that there is a financial dealing between the dishonest bank officials with the Siemens because, they did not raise any objection that it was not the stipulation in the undertaking that they would pay the money on receipt of bill from the Contech. Further it appears that Mr. Rahman has rightly submitted that in view of the admitted position there is no scope to submit any bill by the Contech to Siemens inasmuch as the portion of the share of the Contech has been determined at the time of entering into the contract and the admitted position is that the generator has been installed and on top of that the final bill has also been received by Siemens and Siemens are not carrying out their obligation. Therefore, at the first instance it was a duty of the bank to pursue not the plaintiff-respondents but the real debtor, the Siemens. Mr. Biswas drawing our attention to the letter dated 14.11.2000 written by Siemens to the respondents submitted that in that letter as back as on 14.11.2000 Siemens made it clear to the respondents that they could not make the payment for want of receipt of invoice from Contech. It appears that no copy of this letter was endorsed to the bank. When we put a question to Mr. Biswas how the bank came across that letter, Mr. Biswas stated that this letter was submitted by the present plaintiff-respondents along with their written statement in the Arthorin Adalat case .Then also it smacks of mala fide on the part of the bank. Because, before the submission of the written statement the bank had no knowledge of this letter. Then a question automatically crops up and that is that why the bank maintained a long silence about the contention raised by the Siemens in their earlier two letters. They could have asked the Siemens to liquidate the liability as per undertaking and/or to be on the safe side to bring it to the notice of the plaintiff-respondents but they did nothing. They have neither written to the Siemens that they cannot stop the payment on this plea nor Siemens were not made a party in that case and this circumstance lends support to the contention that there was and is an understanding with the bank officials and the Siemens Bangladesh Ltd to allow Siemens to reap undue advantage by using the money of the plaintiffs. It is further pointed out by Mr. Khalilur Rahman that since the undertaking is still in force and was in force on the date of institution of the Arthorin Adalat case the bank could well ask the Siemens to make payment and on their refusal they could have instituted the Arthorin Adalat case impleading them. We do not find any reason for not impleading Siemens in the Arthorin Case. So, the one sided correspondence made between the Siemens and the bank is nothing but are products of fraud committed upon the plaintiffs by them to victimize the present plaintiff-respondents. 

 13. From our discussions aforesaid it has become clear that though the instant suit has been filed by the plaintiff-respondents amongst other, with a prayer for money decree but in fact it touches interest of the plaintiff-respondents in immovable property which have been mortgaged to the Bank. Therefore, in view of the facts and circumstances of the case if the defendant-appellant is allowed to proceed with the execution of the Arthorin decree and at the end of the day if the instant suit is decreed in favour of the plaintiff-respondents they would not be able to regain the possession of the mortgaged property and thus in the facts and circumstances of the case it appears to us that the balance of convenience and inconvenience is also in favour of the respondents and the injury will be an irreparable one. 

 14. Mr. Mrinal Kanti Biswas in the course of argument very emphatically urged before us that if the impugned order is Maintained that will unnecessarily delay the execution of the Arthorin Adalat decree. No doubt if the impugned order is maintained that will definitely delay the proceedings of the execution case but it appears to us that the defendant-appellant is also responsible for the delay inasmuch as in the Arthorin suit the definite case of the plaintiff-respondents was that in view of the clear undertaking given by the Siemens it was the legal obligation of the bank to pursue their claim primarily against the Siemens but they have not impleaded them in the Arthorin Adalat case which in the facts and circumstances of the present case, compelled the plaintiff-respondents to file the instant suit to protect their legal right. Therefore, that cannot, in our opinion, be a valid ground to interfere with the impugned order. 

 15. Another point which was emphatically urged by Mr. Biswas was that in the injunction petition the plaintiff-respondents-opposite partiers sought for an injunction against defendant Nos. 2-3 of the instant suit not to proceed with the Arthorin Execution Case No. 338 of 2004 but the Trial Court has passed an order against the defendant-appellant to maintain status quo in respect of the suit property and on that ground he urged upon us to interfere with the impugned order. Earlier we had discussed the back grounds of the case and on perusal of the application it appears that the injunction application was filed under order 39, rules 1 and 2 read with section 151 of the Code and in fact the plaintiff-respondents made a clear prayer for restraining the defendant Nos. 1 and 2, i.e., the present appellants not to proceed with the aforesaid execution case but the Trial Court in his wisdom passed an order against the defendants asking them to maintain status 'quo in respect of the suit property. It is now well settled that an order of status quo in its legal parlance means an order of injunction and although the Trial Court by the impugned order asked the defendant-appellants to maintain status quo that, in fact, gave the temporary relief which has been sought for by the plaintiff-respondents in their application for injunction. Besides, it is now well settled that the civil court can in an appropriate case couch its order in such terms as it deems fit and proper in the given facts and circumstances of the case. On a scrutiny of the impugned order and the prayer made by the plaintiffs in their application we find that by the impugned order substantially the defendant-appellant has been restrained in fact not to proceed with the aforesaid Arthorin Execution Case filed by the defendant-appellant before the Arthorin Adalat. In this regard Mr. Khalilur Rahman has cited the decision reported in PLD 1954 (Lahore) 414 wherein it has been laid down that although a court cannot restrain another court by granting an injunction not to proceed with the judicial proceedings but nevertheless parties of the suit can be restrained by an order of injunction not to proceed with the case. In the case reported in AIR 1953 (Calcutta) 377 it has been laid down that there is nothing in section 56 of the Specific Relief Act to persuade the court from restraining a party to proceed with judicial proceedings. In the case reported in AIR 1931 (Calcutta) 279 it has been held that injunction under section 56 does not persuade any Court from making an order in personel forbidding proceedings in another court even if such person is out the court jurisdiction. The same view has been reiterated by the Rajasthan High Court within the Indian jurisdiction in the case reported in AIR 1977 (Rajasthan) 191 wherein it has been laid down in clear terms that temporary injunction can be granted for restraining a party from proceedings with the execution of decree. Therefore, if the propriety of the impugned order is judged in the light of the aforesaid decisions we do not find any elements of illegality or impropriety in the impugned order on that count. More so, when Mr. Biswas could not lay his hands on any decision which takes a different view on the point. 

 16. Now let us advert to the decisions referred by Mr. Biswas in support of his contention that the impugned order cannot be sustained in view of the principles of law which is well settled in respect of granting temporary injunction. In support of his contention he has relied on a decision reported in 17 BLD (HCD) 204 wherein one of us was a party. On a reading of the same it appears to us that in that case it was observed that mere presence of a prima facie case or arguability thereof will not by itself be a ground for issuing temporary injunction. The existence of a prima facie case, the irreparability of loss and balance of convenience and inconvenience must co-exist before granting temporary injunction. These are the principles which are deep rooted not only within our jurisdiction but in all other jurisdictions in the matter of temporary injunction and none including Mr. Rahman did say a single word against the principle of law laid down in this decision. But from our discussion in the aforesaid paragraphs we have made it clear that all the three main elements of temporary injunction are found to be present in the instant case. Therefore, this decision, in fact, does not help Mr. Biswas. 

 17. Mr. Biswas then relied on the decision reported in 15 BLD(AD) 47. In that case our Appellate Division observed that if the petitioner files successive suits to frustrate the decree obtained in an earlier suit the prayer for stay of the further proceedings of the execution case is liable to be rejected as' being not bone fide. In the instant case while addressing the issue as to the prima facie case we had made it clear that the instant suit is a bona fide one filed by the plaintiff-respondents to safeguard their interest in the compelling circumstances and from the materials on record by no stretch of imagination it could be said that the instant suit is mala fide one. Thus, this case is also of little or no assistance to Mr. Biswas. Finally Mr. Biswas to substantiate his contention relied on yet another decision of our Appellate Division as reported in 33 DLR (AD) 298 and relying on this decision he urged upon us that it is now well settled that there cannot be any injunction for actionable wrongs for which damages are adequate remedy. So is the view taken by our Appellate Division in the case reported in 29 DLR (SC) 82 and there is no dispute about the principles of law in this regard. We have already addressed this issue earlier and came to a finding that in the instant case non-granting of injunction, in the facts and circumstances of the case, will cause irreparable loss. Therefore, these cases, in our view, are not attracted in the facts and circumstances of the instant case. Mr. Biswas drawing our attention to the provisions of section 37 of the Arthorin Adalat Act submitted that a time frame of 90 days has been laid down by the Parliament for completion of execution proceedings in Arthorin Adalat Case and the provisions of section 37 if read in conjunction with the preamble of the enactment leads us to the irresistible conclusion that this special form was created by the Parliament with the sole intention to settle the disputes between the financial institutions on the one hand and the borrowers on the other as expeditiously as possible and that is why a time frame has been imposed upon the Arthorin Adalat in that regard and if that aspect of the law is kept in mind it is found that the impugned order negates the purpose and scheme of Arthorin Adalat and in exercise of discretionary power any court should keep in the back of their mind the purpose of the enactment and in that view of the matter also the impugned order cannot be sustained on the scrutiny of law and the attempt made by the bank for realizing its dues from the defaulter plaintiff-respondents would fall to the ground for no fault of them. In this connection Mr. Biswas also referred to the provisions of section 55 of the Arthorin Adalat Ain wherein it has been stated that the Arthorin Adalat shall be under the direct administrative control of the District Judge and under the indirect supervision and control of the High Court Division and relying on these provisions he wants to say that since the Authorin Adalat is neither a civil court nor under the supervision and control of any civil court, no civil court has jurisdiction to pass any order including an order of injunction. We have weighed this submission very seriously and taking into consideration the facts and circumstances of the case we find that the learned Trial Court under the compelling circumstances in the interest of justice and fair play had no other alternative but to pass the said order in the peculiarity of the facts and circumstances of the instant case. In this connection it may further be mentioned that the general administration of the Arthorin Adalat is not in issue and as we have already indicated that by the impugned order the Arthorin Adalat has not been restrained by an order of injunction or status quo not to proceed with the execution case rather it is the decree-holder who has been restrained by the impugned order to maintain status quo untill the disposal of the suit.
